messages.author: 786a24990da9e91c
messages.subject: NA and data organisation
parts:
Hi Stan community,
currently I'm trying to migrate a model from JAGS to Stan and I would highly appreciate any hint or comment to my problem. As I am using an adaptive choice task, trial length differs between subjects. For JAGS I organized my data in the way that a matrix contain the data of all subjects and the unused fields are filled with NA. I then loop through only the filled matrix cells during sampling. I tried to implement this in Stan like this: 

data {
  int ns1; # number of participants
  int nt1_max; # maximum number of trials
  int nt1[ns1]; # number of trials per subject
  int choice1[ns1,nt1_max];
  real delay_diff1[ns1,nt1_max];
  real amount1[ns1,nt1_max];
  real amount_now1[ns1,nt1_max];
}

[...]

transformed parameters {
  matrix<lower=0>[ns1,nt1_max] sv1;
  matrix<lower=0, upper=1>[ns1,nt1_max] p1;

  for (i in 1:ns1){
    for (j in 1:nt1[i]){
      sv1[i,j] <- amount1[i,j] / (1 + k1[i]* delay_diff1[i,j]);
        p1[i,j] <- exp(sv1[i,j]/temp1[i]) / ((exp(amount_now1[i,j]/temp1[i])) + exp(sv1[i,j]/temp1[i]));
    }
  }
}

[...]

After translating and compiling the model I get the following error message:

Error in FUN(c("ns1", "nt1", "nt1_max", "delay_diff1", "amount1", "amount_now1", : Stan does not support NA (in delay_diff1) in data
failed to preprocess the data; sampling not done

I tried to replace the NA fields with 99999, but that seems to not solve my problem:

Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : 
  Error during user-specified initialization:
Invalid value of sv1: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: sv1[1]  is nan:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

Does any of you has I hint for me how I organize my data in a way that Stan is able to sample from the model? That would be very helpful for me. Any comment is highly appreciated!

Cheers,
Antonius

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NA and data organisation
parts:
Hi Antonius,

Elements of matrices in Stan are initialized to NaN. In the transformed parameters block, you've declared sv1 as a matrix with a lower bound as 0. You'll need to set the remaining elements of sv1 to something greater or equal to 0, even if they aren't used.



Daniel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: NA and data organisation
parts:
Replacing the NAs with 99999 is the way to go but you then have to be very careful to never use a 99999 in a calculation. Basically, you need to declare in the parameters block a vector of unknowns whose length is equal to the number of NA values. Then in the model block make a hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector, that uses the data when it is observed and pulls from the vector of unknowns when the data is 99999. That hybrid can be used for a complete data likelihood and you should also model the probability that an observation is NA, presumably as a function of the hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector. However, this is all moot if you have missingness on discrete valued data because Stan does not permit you to declare discrete unknowns in the parameter block. Maybe just maybe you can do some data augmentation thing where you have continuous unknowns underlying discrete observables, but that is going to be tedious at best.

Basically, Stan sucks at the sort of missing data problems that are commonplace in practice and this is the one area where the BUGS family of software has the biggest advantage over Stan. Although such models tend to be slow at best with BUGS and have at least as many problems with convergence, mixing, etc. as models for fully observed data.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: NA and data organisation
parts:
I think using magic number codings is confusing and also
fragile.

If possible, using the same kind of technique as for sparse
matrices may be clearer and less error prone and also tighter
in memory and runtime depending on the amount of missingness.

So if you have a vector y of size N, but it has some missingness,
then you create four arrays,

y_obs[N_obs];
idx_obs[N_obs];

y_miss[N_miss];
idx_miss[N_miss];

where the idea is that y[idx_miss[n]] = y_obs[n] and similarly
for y_miss.

I would recommend reading Michael's outline of the problem, too,
which I cut out and put into the next manual issue so I can include a version
in the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/786#issuecomment-56707484

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: NA and data organisation
parts:
You need to make sure p1[i,j] is defined to have a value before
calling
choice1[i,j] ~ bernoulli(p1[i,j]);

Unlike BUGS/JAGS, Stan is imperative and executes statements in
order.

If you want more specific advice, you'll need to send us your full
model.

- Bob

parts:
Metropolis rejection aren't a problem as long as they occur only early during initialization / warmup when Stan is still adjusting the stepsize of the sampling algorithm (stepping outside the support of parameters leads to a Metropolis rejection). If you get these messages (it's not an error) during sampling, your model may be ill-conditioned and you need to find out what's causing it.

Just to check: did you intend to use gamma priors for the standard deviations. The way you parameterized them (ultra-vague prior) is reminiscent of inverse-gamma distribution as conjugate prior for variance. However, these priors usually have to much mass close to zero (which I guess is why you truncated them). In BUGS, the normal distribution is specified in terms of mean and precision; in Stan, it's mean and standard deviation, so in your model the prior is not conjugate. You might just as well use a half-Cauchy prior for standard deviation (no truncation needed as long as the support in the parameters block is lower=0 and the hyperparameters of the prior are fixed).

The truncation in your code leads to another thing: you don't need to do it if it you've defined the support of the parameter AND the parameters feeding into the desired truncated distribution are fixed. Truncation will add something to the log-posterior, and if the parameters of the truncated distribution are fixed, the addition will be constant (so totally unnecessary). I.e. you can drop the truncations in the priors for standard deviations.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: NA and data organisation
parts:
Hm tricky one as I'm not familiar with the model itself. Some further observations:

  • you can drop the truncation on the statements like temp1_mu ~ normal(2.5624,2.0327)T[0,] as the parameters are fixed, so the truncation only adds a constant to the log-posterior. Statements like k1[i] ~ normal(k1_mu,k1_lambda)T[0,] do need the truncation as the parameters aren't fixed, so truncation adds a non-constant number to the log-posterior, which is important for the gradient.
  • ah, the cause of your Metropolis rejections is that you have defined the support for k1_mu and k3_mu to be <lower=0>, whereas the priors do not cover only part of the positive real numbers. So what happens is that on the unconstrained scale, the sampler samples a number, exponentiates it to satisfy the support <lower=0> (and adds the Jacobian of the transformation to the posterior to correct the curvature), and then sometimes finds that the density doesn't exist because you tell the model that the density does not exist outside the range of the priors in the model block. Fix: match the support in the parameter block with the domain that your prior in your model block covers. Once you've done this, you can even leave out the prior from the model block if it's uniform, as this is the standard in Stan (i.e. if you specify the support in the parameter block to be <lower=-1,upper=1>, you effectively say that the parameter has a uniform distribution between -1 and 1, unless you specify a prior in the model block that says otherwise. The manual should provide insight into the mechanics behind this).

In BUGS, the normal distribution is specified in terms of mean and precision; in Stan, it's mean and standard deviation, so in your model the prior is not conjugate. You might just as well use a half-Cauchy prior for standard deviation (no truncation needed as long as the support in the parameters block is lower=0 and the hyperparameters of the prior are fixed).

The truncation in your code leads to another thing: you don't need to do it if it you've defined the support of the parameter AND the parameters feeding into the desired truncated distribution are fixed. Truncation will add something to the log-posterior, and if the parameters of the truncated distribution are fixed, the addition will be constant (so totally unnecessary). I.e. you can drop the truncations in the priors for standard deviations.

> > Replacing the NAs with 99999 is the way to go but you then have to be very careful to never use a 99999 in a calculation. Basically, you need to declare in the parameters block a vector of unknowns whose length is equal to the number of NA values. Then in the model block make a hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector, that uses the data when it is observed and pulls from the vector of unknowns when the data is 99999. That hybrid can be used for a complete data likelihood and you should also model the probability that an observation is NA, presumably as a function of the hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector. However, this is all moot if you have missingness on discrete valued data because Stan does not permit you to declare discrete unknowns in the parameter block. Maybe just maybe you can do some data augmentation thing where you have continuous unknowns underlying discrete observables, but that is going to be tedious at best.
> >
> > Basically, Stan sucks at the sort of missing data problems that are commonplace in practice and this is the one area where the BUGS family of software has the biggest advantage over Stan. Although such models tend to be slow at best with BUGS and have at least as many problems with convergence, mixing, etc. as models for fully observed data.
